tweets.text:
Zach on refounding Ro after five years of building

“The best company cultures are strong attract, strong repel. It knows who it is, and it continues to try and double down on the features and eliminate the bugs.”

Lessons and surprising stats from how they did it:
- Ro has patients in every US county but one: Kalawao County, Hawaii, population 82

- In December 2021, Ro was growing 9% a year at a $270M run rate

- Today Ro is at a $3B+ run rate after growing 100%+ a year for three years

- It did that with fewer people, going from 463 to 406

- ARR per employee is up more than 10x

- 95 of the first 100 hires were people the founders already knew

- Ro parted with ~7 VPs, then let go of ~20% of the company

- Everyone was asked to opt in or opt out of the new culture, and 6–8% left

- The founders met with top talent for breakfast, lunch and dinner for 30 straight days

- They gave top performers more equity and asked for 90 days. If nothing changed, they’d help them find their next job

Zach on refounding Ro after five years of building

“The best company cultures are strong attract, strong repel. It knows who it is, and it continues to try and double down on the features and eliminate the bugs.”

Lessons and surprising stats from how they did it:
- Ro has patients in every US county but one: Kalawao County, Hawaii, population 82

- In December 2021, Ro was growing 9% a year at a $270M run rate

- Today Ro is at a $3B+ run rate after growing 100%+ a year for three years

- It did that with fewer people, going from 463 to 406

- ARR per employee is up more than 10x

- 95 of the first 100 hires were people the founders already knew

- Ro parted with ~7 VPs, then let go of ~20% of the company

- Everyone was asked to opt in or opt out of the new culture, and 6–8% left

- The founders met with top talent for breakfast, lunch and dinner for 30 straight days

- They gave top performers more equity and asked for 90 days. If nothing changed, they’d help them find their next job

- Ro shut down 10+ products and cut $50M+ of unprofitable revenue

Mike: “It is much bigger, but in the 100,000 feet abstraction, what is it that is being built? Back then it was communication that was being built. Today we’re building intelligence. And the economic value of intelligence is probably higher than the economic value of communication.”

“I also think that, believe it or not, it’s been nearly 30 years, the markets are more efficient now, which is why so much more risk capital is willing to make its way into AI.”

“So net is, I’m actually more optimistic about this cycle, but I also believe that there will be some correction and some cleaning up of the industry structure.”

@appenz @mavolpi

US pension funds are heavily concentrated in technology stocks:

The technology sector accounts for 44% of total US pension fund equity allocation, according to a Bloomberg analysis of more than 70 pension funds.

This percentage has more than doubled since 2015.

Pension fund equity allocation to technology is now larger than that of the next 3 sectors combined.

By comparison, Financials represent 16%, followed by Healthcare at 12%, Industrials at 11%, and Consumer stocks at 10%.

To put this into perspective, the Consumer sector was these funds' largest allocation in 2014, at ~20%.

US pension funds are more exposed to technology stocks than ever.

Americans are worried about their jobs.

The Machine Learning market is seeing accelerating growth.

The global machine learning market is now projected to grow from ~$100 billion in 2025 to ~$684 billion by 2033.

This implies a CAGR of +27.2% from 2025 to 2033.

As AI evolves, the focus is shifting toward AI models that can continuously learn, retain knowledge, and adapt to new tasks.

This represents a fundamental shift from AI systems that rely primarily on knowledge acquired during training to systems capable of improving through experience.

As adoption accelerates, demand for machine learning software, hardware, and services is expected to increase substantially.

We are watching this market.

I've been in crypto for 10 years now, and I've seen several bull markets and bear markets.

This is what the bottom looks like.

The timeline is filled with defeat, despair, disgust, disdain, and disinterest.

It happens every time, and every time it does... we find a way through.

New opportunities present themselves. New narratives emerge.

And the craziest part? It usually happens all at once.

You go from absolute zero to mach 5 in the blink of an eye.

If you're sidelined when that happens, you're usually left sidelined praying the market eventually slows down to give you the entry you had at the lows.

So while everyone else capitulates - strap in.

Patient bulls will continue to thrive.

I could always be wrong, but I do believe I have a coherent thesis.

Robinhood Chain is early and expect its growth to outpace most L1s/L2s this cycle.

Robinhood is the og home of retail trading + memes.

Cat coins are undervalued,and have a huge opportunity gap I believe will be filled this cycle.

Market is at the bottom. Anything that survives and manages to grow now has a massive advantage when the broader crypto eco starts pumping again.

Lore of the chain is still being defined. Put in the work early and the growth of the eco itself usually takes over at a certain point.

e.g. already have seen some of that early work pay off by being recognized on the RH assets list.

I believe the team organically starts actually listing names from that list for trading in app when the market picks back up.

And I also believe in the power of concentrated attention and capital. I’ve seen a lot of the names you’ve listed amongst almost every other person on CT diffuse both with a million new names every day silently dropping the others.

I’ve tried to do things differently.

FinCEN = Financial Crimes Enforcement Network. They’re part of the U.S. Treasury Department and focus on money laundering, terrorist financing, and other financial crimes.

They’re the ones accusing @MEXC of facilitating illicit transactions, and they’ve issued an order restricting its access to the U.S. financial system.

So there’s more behind this than Binance just not liking MEXC.

FinCEN’s order takes effect December 10, but Binance has already introduced its restrictions.

And transfers to MEXC will be rejected, while deposits from MEXC will be held for compliance review.

I’m sure Binance has enough to worry about already, so I can see why they’re keeping their distance.

This aged pretty well, when I said this last year in 2025, Clickhouse was a $6.7B company... 

Now as an update, their secondary valuation sits around ~$50B, which $NBIS owns 25%+ of. 

I've always liked Nebius the most because sum of parts, with all their lesser known subsidiaries growing alongside their core neocloud business.

Including Avride (self-driving), Clickhouse, Toloka, and other subsidiaries that they owned.  

This year Nebius also acquired:
- Tavily (web search and retrival)
- Clarifai (Inference orchestration)

Which scale independently as well (the others were integrated into Nebius Token Factory).

Hard to view $NBIS as just another neocloud when it has billions in scaling value outside its core infrastructure business.

Builders who are comfortable with that get a much faster way into Hyperliquid’s markets.

tweets.text:
Revenue and buybacks are one of the biggest token narratives of the next cycle.

We've already seen the attention Hyperliquid, Pump. fun, and other protocols have attracted by connecting actual business revenue to their tokens.

If a protocol is generating millions in fees, why shouldn't some of that value flow back to its tokenholders instead of relying on endless emissions?

I expect more projects to move in this direction. One example is @katana, which is making some pretty significant changes to how $KAT works.

The biggest one is a shift toward revenue-funded buybacks.

• Katana has acquired three pieces of its DeFi infrastructure:

• Katana Swap (Sushi deployment) for spot trading

• Katana Perps (IDEX) for leveraged trading

• Vault Bridge for earning yield on bridged assets

Add sequencer fees, and that's four revenue streams feeding into the ecosystem.

Those fees help fund automatic $KAT buybacks, and 100% of the bought-back tokens go to avKAT stakers

The old voting and locking system is also being phased out. You simply stake $KAT, rewards compound automatically, and the unstaking cooldown drops from 45 days to 7.

Of course, buybacks alone don't make a token a good investment. 

The real question is how much revenue these products can generate and how consistently that translates into buybacks.

But I do think the direction is worth watching.

The next cycle might put more weight on what protocols actually earn, and how much of it reaches tokenholders.

tweets.text:
“ai has made content worthless”

true, but that means 99% of what you read is worthless, so how do you build a brand?

having distribution is like owning gold in a world of slop so: here’s how to build a brand that pays you: 👇

1: anyone can prompt a thread in 10 seconds now. the one thing AI can't fake is proof.

2: most accounts don't die from bad hooks. they die because they've got nothing worth saying.

3: so stop asking "what should I post?" and ask "what have I done that's worth posting about?"

4: got a real result? show the numbers and how you got there. failures count too.

5: no results? even better. do an unreasonable amount of work in public. people love watching someone else do the grind.

6: here’s an example, I saw one guy that logged 112 of a trader's streams. 211 hours. he then wrote one article on it- boom, a million impressions and 3,234 bookmarks.

7: my biggest article did 8.96m views for the same reason. I did the boring work so nobody else had to.

8: the hook writes itself: reps + time window + payoff. "I tested 40 workflows for 60 days. here are the 3 that stayed."

9: so pick one painful task your audience avoids. do it for 30 days. publish the data on day 30.

that's proof. and it’s crazy that no-one thinks about the next point in any detail.

10: who are you actually talking to? growing market, real pain, money to spend.

11: on X your words do the targeting. post about everything and you get shown to nobody.

12: write one sentence naming your person, their pain and what they'd pay for. can't? don't post yet.

13: then you condition them. same pfp, same cover style, same format, for a whole year.

14: this is where most people quit. it feels boring. but boring is exactly why it works.

15: list the 5 things your audience loves and put them in 80% of your posts.

16: list 3 things they hate and stand against them publicly.

and here's the bit that decides if they ever come back:

17: hooks get someone to try you once. your work decides if they come back.

18: on X the free stuff is your work. if your title promises a playbook, it had better be one.

19: 10/10 marketing on 4/10 content just kills you.

20: best thing anyone's ever said about my work was a reply: "I passed my cert today!", and that was on an article I wrote on becoming a Claude architect.

21: do great work, give more than you promised, repeat for weeks, then months, then years.

22: once it works, defend it with big public moments. a goal, a deadline, real stakes. proof is everything.

23: build in public, and grow in public. 

24: the 90 days: month 1 proof, month 2 your person, month 3 ship what you were working towards and announce the big moment, if you’re smart you can turn this in to newsletter sign ups and distribute it through here. 

25: you can keep polishing hooks with nothing behind them, or go do the work that makes the hook true.

I'm writing the full article on this today: every level, the homework and what I use.

follow or turn notifications on so you don't miss it 😜

Some fun: When has the market looked like this before?

I took the current cross-asset regime — equities, rates, credit, FX, commodities and volatility — and compared it with historical 63-trading-day periods based on both the direction and magnitude of market moves.

The closest historical match to November 2026?

April 2005 — 81% similarity.

What I found especially interesting is that it passes the macro smell test as well. Both periods combine relatively strong growth, elevated inflation, restrictive/tightening conditions, a fairly flat positive yield curve and credit markets that are not signaling acute stress.

That does not mean 2026 = 2005. There are some very important differences, particularly around housing and equity valuations.

So I also looked at what happened after the closest historical regimes.

Across the closest analogues, the median S&P 500 path was:

+2.0% after 1 month
+5.7% after 3 months
+3.4% after 6 months
+11.6% after 12 months
But the individual paths vary enormously — which is really the point.

Historical analogues aren't forecasts. They are a way of asking: when markets have been pricing a similar combination of growth, inflation, rates, credit and risk before, what happened next?

Still experimenting with this, but I think there is something pretty interesting here.

$ZIM : 𝗔 𝗦𝗮𝗳𝗲 𝗛𝗮𝗿𝗯𝗼𝗿

𝗪𝗵𝘆 ZIM 𝗜𝘀 𝟯𝟬% 𝗼𝗳 𝗠𝘆 𝗣𝗼𝗿𝘁𝗳𝗼𝗹𝗶𝗼 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗠𝘆 𝗟𝗮𝗿𝗴𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗛𝗼𝗹𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴

The chart below shows just how disconnected $ZIM’s stock price is from its underlying economic value. By year-end, I estimate the company will have approximately $32 per share in cash, yet the stock trades at just $29. That makes very little economic sense to me, especially when you consider the value of its vessels, containers, shipping contracts, and profitable operating business, even after accounting for its liabilities.

And that’s before the approximately 20% dividend yield I expect over the next four to five months.

𝗜. 𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗱𝗶𝗱 𝘄𝗲 𝗴𝗲𝘁 𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲?

The previous management ran $ZIM like a Trojan horse. The former CEO, CFO, and a board that allowed this to happen created a situation that could have made insiders billionaires through a cheap takeover.

The former CEO used every opportunity to keep $ZIM’s stock price low and guide analysts toward pessimistic expectations, while building up extraordinary amounts of cash on the balance sheet and structuring questionable deals. In my view, the plan was to acquire $ZIM for around $25 per share, effectively using the massive cash reserves he had accumulated inside the company to finance the takeover.

Look at the charter agreements (second tweet below). Some vessels cost over $90,000 per day, with rates scheduled to drop to around $8,000 after two to two and a half years, exactly after the management buyout would have occurred. Historical earnings looked terrible, while the buyer would inherit dramatically lower costs.

The former CEO and CFO are out. The original plan didn’t work out as expected. Now shareholders have an opportunity to benefit from the economics that were waiting on the other side.

𝗜𝗜. 𝗔𝗻𝗰𝗵𝗼𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗶𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗹𝗲𝗺.

The $35 Hapag-Lloyd offer has become an artificial ceiling in investors’ minds. People stopped calculating what $ZIM is worth and started measuring everything against $35.

That is a serious mistake.

𝗜𝗜𝗜. $𝟯𝟱 𝗶𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗹 𝗮𝗰𝗾𝘂𝗶𝘀𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗽𝗿𝗶𝗰𝗲.

Hapag-Lloyd’s effective cost is closer to $50 per share after accounting for FIMI, employee compensation, intermediaries, and other transaction costs.

Maersk reportedly offered $32, with additional costs of its own. MSC was also interested, according to Samer Haj-Yehia.

There was real competition for this company.

𝗜𝗩. 𝗡𝗼𝗯𝗼𝗱𝘆 𝗽𝗮𝘆𝘀 $𝟱𝟬 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗮 𝗯𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝘁𝗵 𝗼𝗻𝗹𝘆 $𝟱𝟬.

I estimate Hapag-Lloyd valued $ZIM at $70 or more. Nobody enters such a complicated transaction, involving Israel’s golden share and political approvals, without expecting a substantial margin of safety.

𝗩. 𝗦𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗼𝗳𝗳𝗲𝗿, $𝗭𝗜𝗠 𝗵𝗮𝘀 𝗯𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲 𝗳𝗮𝗿 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝘃𝗮𝗹𝘂𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲.

Cash has increased, asset values have risen, and liabilities have remained broadly unchanged.

My estimate is that economic equity value has increased by more than $35 per share since the offer. At current spot rates, I estimate the company adds over $1 per share in economic value every week.

𝗩𝗜. 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗺𝗮𝗿𝗸𝗲𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝗺𝗶𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝗽𝗼𝘁 𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗲𝘅𝗽𝗼𝘀𝘂𝗿𝗲.

Since the offer, Maersk has delivered approximately 36% total return, while $ZIM’s stock has remained flat.

Yet $ZIM is far more exposed to spot freight rates. Its two most important routes, Asia to the U.S. East Coast and West Coast, have seen freight indices rise approximately 246% and 234% in the chart.

The company benefiting most from these increases is the one whose stock hasn’t moved.

𝗩𝗜𝗜. 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗼𝗽𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗯𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝗶𝘀 𝗲𝗳𝗳𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲𝗹𝘆 𝘃𝗮𝗹𝘂𝗲𝗱 𝗯𝗲𝗹𝗼𝘄 𝘇𝗲𝗿𝗼.

Based on my estimates, subtracting cash and net asset values from market capitalization leaves a negative value for the operating business.

Investors are effectively getting a profitable global shipping operation for free.

The recent conversation between @evanspiegel and shareholders on X is a very welcome development.

If you’re observant, you’ll notice some negatives. Evan is clearly not ready to spin out Specs, and he continues to justify stock-based compensation as a necessary tool for acquiring talent. That argument makes sense, although it doesn’t necessarily benefit shareholders.

But there’s something much more important here. Evan Spiegel is apparently reading what people are saying about $SNAP on X. That means he’s seeing the criticism, the frustration and the arguments made by activist shareholders. He knows exactly what people believe is wrong with the company and its stock price.

We’ve never really seen this kind of engagement from him before. He doesn’t need to have these conversations. Nobody is forcing him to respond to shareholders on X. Yet he’s choosing to do so.

That doesn’t guarantee anything will change. But based on my understanding of human nature, I find it very encouraging. People don’t voluntarily engage with criticism unless they care about what’s being said, at least to some degree.

He has made it clear that he cares about shareholders and wants the stock price to be higher. And if he’s reading the criticism, which he apparently is, he knows what needs to change.

I have faith that Evan Spiegel will eventually do the right thing, and I believe $SNAP will be in a very different place 12 months from now.

Most dashboards tell you what moved. The Radar on the Helios Analytics crypto terminal tells you what moved abnormally.

Every asset is scored against its own history, price and fundamentals (fees, revenue, TVL, volume), so a move is judged by how unusual it is for that coin rather than how big it looks.

That matters in a month like this one. Only 9 of 182 assets rose and the median coin fell 23%. In absolute terms almost everything looks the same. Relative to their own history, a few stand right out.

THORChain is the fundamental divergence. $RUNE revenue is +3.6 SD vs its 1-year norm, with the 14-day average up 66% in a month and at the 97th percentile of the past year. The price is down 13% over the same 30 days.

BitTorrent is the volume one. $BTT traded $39M on 9 Nov, almost double its 14-day average and +4.1 SD vs its 1-year norm, while the price barely moved (-2.5% for the month).

Neither is a buy signal on its own (a spike can be noise, or one big trade). But when the whole market is red, knowing which numbers are genuinely out of character is a much better place to start.

THORChain is the fundamental divergence. $RUNE revenue is +3.6 SD vs its 1-year norm, with the 14-day average up 66% in a month and at the 97th percentile of the past year. The price is down 13% over the same 30 days.

BitTorrent is the volume one. $BTT traded $39M on 9 Nov, almost double its 14-day average and +4.1 SD vs its 1-year norm, while the price barely moved (-2.5% for the month).

Neither is a buy signal on its own (a spike can be noise, or one big trade). But when the whole market is red, knowing which numbers are genuinely out of character is a much better place to start.

tweets.text:
Google has unveiled TPU 8i Max, aka Whalefish. One interesting detail is that the announcement confirms the 8i Max will have 384GB of HBM per chip, meaning it moves to 8-hi HBM compared to the 12-hi HBM used for the original TPU 8i, which we reported to Accelerator Model subscribers several months ago. This follows Nvidia's move to move to 8-hi HBM for next generation Rubin Ultra.

Google is advertising much stronger inference performance TPU 8i Max as each package now has double the HBM bandwidth. Bandwidth is more important than capacity for inference performance as we explained recently in our 4-hi HBM article which you can read here: https://t.co/HBWMhtJzy6
